source_theorems.label: Ordinary limits and upper no-regret: a derived reconciliation
source_theorems.pages: printed p.2 / PDF p.14, no-regret paragraph and ordinary lim display
source_theorems.math: \begin{aligned}R_T(u)&=\sum_{t<T}\bigl(\ell_t(x_t)-\ell_t(u)\bigr).\\ \mathrm{Upper}&:\ \forall u\in V\ \forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists N(u,\varepsilon)\ \forall T\ge N:\ R_T(u)/T\le\varepsilon.\\ \mathrm{Literal}&:\ \forall u\in V\ \exists a_u\in\mathbb R:\ a_u\le0,\quad R_T(u)/T\to a_u.\\ \mathrm{Literal}&\Longrightarrow\mathrm{Upper}.\\ \bigl[\forall u\in V\ \exists a_u\in\mathbb R:\ R_T(u)/T\to a_u\bigr]&\Longrightarrow(\mathrm{Literal}\iff\mathrm{Upper}).\\ F(T)&=\begin{cases}T&T\text{ even},\\0&T\text{ odd},\end{cases}\quad \ell_t(x)=(F(t+1)-F(t))x,\quad x_t=0.\\ R_T(u)&=-F(T)u\le0\quad(u\in[0,1]),\\ R_{2(n+1)}(1)/(2(n+1))&=-1,\quad R_{2n+1}(1)/(2n+1)=0.\end{aligned}
source_theorems.plain: The source describes regret as at most sublinear for every fixed comparator and prints an ordinary lim inequality. The library keeps that display distinct from eventual upper-epsilon control. An existing finite limit is nonpositive under upper control. Conversely, a nonpositive finite limit implies upper control. A single fixed affine loss stream shows that upper control alone need not produce an ordinary limit.
source_theorems.fallback: For each fixed comparator, convergence to some finite nonpositive value implies eventual upper-epsilon control. The reverse implication requires actual finite convergence for every comparator. A feasible zero learner on one fixed signed affine loss stream has normalized regret -1 at positive even horizons and0 at odd horizons for comparator1, while upper control holds for every comparator in[0,1].
source_theorems.relationship: Orabona v10 printed p.2/PDF p.14 explicitly uses ordinary lim, not limsup. The eventual-upper interpretation follows the upper-growth wording. The convergence bridges and affine counterexample are derived support that preserves this distinction. The added convergence premise is part of the derived equivalence theorem, not an assumption silently inserted into the source definition.

contract.model: The source has predictions and fixed comparators in V contained in a finite-dimensional real vector space, real losses evaluable there, and online predictions independent of the comparator. Its footnote allows predictions in W containing V in some settings, which requires losses evaluable on W. The generic Lean bridge uses one supplied trace on arbitrary X with total losses Nat -> X -> Real and comparator set V. This admits a W trace when W is contained in X and losses are defined on X, but it neither enforces feasibility/causality nor constructs an algorithm or a uniform guarantee over all loss sequences. In the concrete counterexample, x_t=0 is feasible and independent of outcomes, comparator and horizon.
contract.assumptions: For the ordinary-to-upper implication, every fixed u in V has a finite real limit a_u<=0. For the reverse implication, actual convergence for each u is supplied explicitly and upper control determines its sign. Threshold N(u,epsilon) and limit a_u may depend on u and the supplied trace. Negative limits are allowed; no uniform comparator threshold, absolute convergence, nonnegative regret or zero-limit claim follows. No IID, expectation, filtration or convexity assumption is used in these generic trace bridges.
contract.parameters: Regret is the signed cumulative difference at the same horizon T. Source rounds1..T map to Lean0..T-1. Real division at T=0 is total in Lean, while the asymptotic condition ignores finite initial horizons. The separating maps 2(n+1) and2n+1 are positive and tend to infinity. Limits are finite real limits, with no implicit extended-real convention.
contract.regret: For F(0)=0, telescoping gives sum_{t<T} ell_t(u)=F(T)u. The zero learner has loss0, so R_T(u)=-F(T)u. F(T)>=0 and u>=0 prove upper control on[0,1]. The coefficients at t=0,1,2,3 are0,2,-2,4 and are unbounded in time. This is an actual infinite signed affine loss stream, not a bounded-loss, squared-loss or meanPredict counterexample.
contract.guarantee: If an existing limit a were positive, upper control with epsilon=a/2 and le_of_tendsto would give a<=a/2. Conversely, tendsto_order makes a sequence converging to a_u<=0 eventually less than any positive epsilon. These implications prove equivalence under per-comparator convergence. For the affine stream, the exact telescoping identity gives upper control at all horizons. At u=1, even and odd positive cofinal subsequences converge respectively to-1 and0, so uniqueness of real limits rules out an ordinary limit. The existing strict-past mean predictor has a separate upper guarantee: its same-path empirical-mean minimum bounds each fixed comparator, and (4+4log T)/T tends to0. That producer does not establish ordinary normalized-regret convergence.

source_theorems.fallback: The minimum of expected fixed loss is T times population variance. For the stated causal policies, excess equals the sum of expected squared deviations from the population mean. Average excess divides this finite quantity by a positive horizon.

contract.model: Use a probability measure, measurable observations with one common law, and almost-sure support in [0,1]. Write m = E[Y_0] and v = Var(Y_0). Source round t+1 is Lean index t. contract.assumptions: For the fixed minimum, common law suffices. Causal excess adapters additionally use mutual independence of observations. A history policy is measurable on its full real-history domain, and its output is required to lie in [0,1] on legal interval-valued histories. No bound is imposed on illegal histories. L2 and current-target independence are proved internally for these adapters.
contract.parameters: One common probability space; natural-indexed real observations. T=0 is included in the unnormalized formulas, without a uniqueness assertion. Normalization requires T>0.

These finite identities do not prove sublinear excess, an ordinary regret limit, or coverage of every randomized or filtration-adapted strategy.
contract.guarantee: Bounded support supplies finite second moments. The fixed-comparator decomposition is Tv+T(u-m)^2. Integrating the interval bounds makes m feasible, and nonnegative squared bias makes Tv the actual least loss. For a strict-history policy, measurability and legal-history feasibility supply L2, while mutual independence makes its prediction independent of the current target. The shared square identity then gives expected loss equal to Tv plus the sum of expected squared prediction biases. Subtraction and positive-horizon normalization give the displayed formulas. The source omits these formal bridges; they are derived support, not a verbatim printed proof.

source_theorems.label: Private tape, strict-past information and finite IID excess
source_theorems.pages: printed pp. 1–2 / PDF pp. 13–14: finite expected benchmark, with a derived private-tape extension
source_theorems.math: \begin{aligned}S&\perp(Y_t)_{t\ge0},\qquad\mathcal G_t=\sigma(S,(Y_s)_{s<t}),\\\mathcal F_t&\le\mathcal G_t,\quad P_t\text{ is }\mathcal F_t\text{-measurable},\\B_T&=\inf_{u\in[0,1]}\mathbb E\!\sum_{t<T}(u-Y_t)^2=Tv,\\\Delta_T&=\mathbb E\!\sum_{t<T}(P_t-Y_t)^2-B_T\\&=\sum_{t<T}\mathbb E(P_t-m)^2\ge0.\end{aligned}
source_theorems.plain: The printed source gives a population-variance benchmark for causal guessing. This extension supplies an explicit information model: a private tape independent of the entire IID target process, together with the strict past. Feasible predictions measurable in subordinate information satisfy the finite excess identity.
source_theorems.fallback: Join one whole-process-independent private tape to the strict past. Exact measurable feasible predictions in that information are independent of their current targets; their expected excess is the sum of expected squared deviations from the population mean.
source_theorems.relationship: Derived private-tape extension of the finite expected guessing-game benchmark in Orabona, Online Learning: A Modern Introduction Using Convex Optimization, arXiv:1912.13213v10 (21 June 2026), printed pp. 1–2 / PDF pp. 13–14. Those pages do not give a private-seed or sigma-field theorem or proof.

contract.model: Work on a probability space with measurable real targets Y_t and a measurable private tape S. The target family is mutually independent, and S is independent of the entire target sequence as one random element. Independence from each coordinate separately is insufficient. source_theorems.label: Actual FTL regret and ordinary-limit semantics
source_theorems.plain: Write Phi_T for the squared loss at the horizon empirical mean. The old leader minimizes the length-T prefix. Thus Phi_(T+1) is at most Phi_T plus the actual next loss. Induction from the empty prefix gives Phi_T at most the actual cumulative FTL loss. For positive T, expand squared comparator loss around the empirical mean using the existing exact decomposition. Subtract this from the same cumulative prediction loss. At T=0, all sums vanish. This retains the exact negative squared-distance term. Use the empirical mean to identify the interval-best comparator. The nonnegative gap and the existing bound 4+4 log T squeeze normalized best regret between zero and a quantity tending to zero. At positive horizons, normalized fixed regret equals normalized best regret minus squared distance from the comparator to the empirical mean. The first term tends to zero. Subtract limits in each direction to prove the equivalence. Use the assumed empirical-mean convergence and continuity of the square to obtain the squared-distance limit. Apply the equivalence to get -(u-m)^2 for each real comparator. Nonpositivity then supplies the literal unit-comparator LimitNoRegret witness.
source_theorems.fallback: For the actual squared-loss FTL predictor, cumulative loss is at least the squared loss of the horizon empirical mean, for every real observation stream and every horizon. Signed regret against any fixed real comparator is the empirical-mean regret minus the horizon times a squared distance. When every observation lies in [0,1], the actual best-comparator regret divided by the horizon converges to zero. For unit observations, a fixed-comparator regret limit exists with value a exactly when the squared distance from that comparator to the empirical mean converges to -a. If the empirical mean of a unit-valued stream converges to m, every fixed-comparator normalized regret converges to the explicit nonpositive value -(u-m)^2.

source_theorems.label: A bounded actual-FTL obstruction and exact converse
source_theorems.math: \begin{gathered}\mathrm{LimitNoRegret}(p,y)\Longleftrightarrow\exists m\in[0,1]:\bar y_T\to m,\\ d_t\in[0,1],\qquad\bar d_{4^{n+1}-1}\to\tfrac23,\quad\bar d_{2\cdot4^n-1}\to\tfrac13,\\ \mathrm{UpperNoRegret}(p,d),\quad R_T^{\mathrm{best}}/T\to0,\\ \nexists a\in\mathbb R:R_T(0)/T\to a,\qquad\neg\mathrm{LimitNoRegret}(p,d).\end{gathered}
source_theorems.plain: Use the proposed comparator limits at 0 and 1 and the existing fixed-regret criterion. They give limits for M_T squared and (1-M_T) squared. Their difference plus one, divided by two, equals M_T. Eventual interval membership places the limit in [0,1]. Conversely, empirical-mean convergence yields every comparator limit -(u-m)^2 through the existing FTL producer. Strong induction applies to the strictly smaller parent floor(n/2). The base value is zero; taking one minus a binary value exchanges zero and one. Both outcomes belong to the closed unit interval. The two children at 2k+1 and 2k+2 both equal 1-d_k. Pairing them gives S_(2n+1)=2n-2S_n. Induction yields exact high and low prefix counts. The high mean is exactly 2/3; the low mean is 1/3 minus 1/(3(2*4^n-1)). The two positive natural horizons diverge, so the latter correction tends to zero. Apply the existing actual-FTL upper guarantee and best-regret zero-limit theorem to the proved unit-valued stream. If normalized regret against zero had finite limit a, the existing criterion would force M_T squared to tend to -a. Composition with the two cofinal subsequences forces -a=4/9 and -a=1/9, a contradiction. Since zero is a feasible comparator, LimitNoRegret also fails.
source_theorems.fallback: For every observation stream in [0,1], the actual FTL predictor has a finite nonpositive normalized-regret limit at every fixed comparator in [0,1] exactly when the empirical means converge. The fixed sequence d_0=0 and d_(n+1)=1-d_(floor(n/2)) always lies in [0,1]. Its definition does not depend on a learner or horizon. The same empirical means tend to 2/3 along horizons 4^(n+1)-1 and to 1/3 along horizons 2*4^n-1. On this one bounded stream, the actual FTL predictor has upper-epsilon no-regret and normalized interval-best regret tending to zero, while normalized regret against comparator zero has no finite ordinary limit.

source_theorems.plain: For every positive time, both predictors equal the same strict-prefix empirical mean. Split each cumulative prediction loss into time zero and its tail; the tails cancel. Both best-regret expressions subtract the identical comparator infimum, which cancels without a minimum-existence assumption. The remaining term is c=(a-y_0)^2-(1/2-y_0)^2. Reuse the half-initialized quarter-plus-tail bound and add the exact first-round correction c. Expanding 1/4+c gives a^2+(1-2a)y_0. Since a^2<=a, splitting y_0<=1/2 or y_0>=1/2 bounds this expression by 1. The reciprocal tail is unchanged. For each feasible comparator, its regret is at most the interval-best regret. Combine the exact correction with the half-initialized logarithmic bound. The first squared loss is at most 1, so 5+4 log T is an upper bound for positive T. Divide by T and use 1/T and log T/T tending to zero. The actual proof uses this logarithmic route, not the new finite refined theorem. For positive T, divide the exact identity by T. The accepted half-initialized best-regret theorem gives its normalized limit zero, using an actual nonnegative half-FTL loss gap and an upper bound. The fixed correction c divided by T also tends to zero. Adding these two limits and using eventual equality proves the result; an upper bound alone would not suffice.

proof_bridge.title: From empirical means to regret, initialization and limit obstructions

A first-round identity extends the deterministic guarantees to every legal initialization. The dyadic stream separates best-regret convergence from ordinary fixed-comparator convergence.

steps.title: Empirical minimizers and prefix comparison
steps.detail: Expand both squared-loss sums and use n an=sum yt. The residual is nonnegative and vanishes only at u=an when n>0. Interval feasibility follows by averaging. Let b_n be supplied feasible minimizers of every positive prefix of the arbitrary loss sequence. Cancel the final common summand, apply the induction hypothesis, and use prefix optimality against the feasible final leader. These hindsight leaders are generic; the arithmetic means a_n instantiate them only for squared loss in the following steps.

steps.title: Realize the prefix predictor with an actual recursive state

For the induction step, use the count invariant and the existing all-time empiricalMean_succ identity. The resulting equality S_c(t)=(t,p_c(t)) yields same-initial strict-prefix equality and interval feasibility. At c=1/2 it identifies the trajectory used by the half-initial regret proof. steps.title: Squared-loss benchmark and finite normalization
steps.detail: For independent square-integrable P,Y, use the variance identity and zero covariance. Pointwise support produces L2 for the concrete learner; identical laws align the means and variances before summing. For a probability measure and measurable Y supported pointwise in [0,1], the population mean m = E[Y] belongs to [0,1], E[(m-Y)^2] = Var(Y), and Var(Y) <= E[(u-Y)^2] for every fixed real u. The preserved source_mean_optimal derives these facts from expected_square_decomposition. This identifies the fixed population benchmark; it does not compare the expectation of a random hindsight minimum or give an IID rate. Write L_T = E[sum_{t<T}(p_t-Y_t)^2] and sigma^2 = Var(Y_0). Linearity of the finite integral sum gives the IID identity. Each residual squared-error integral is nonnegative; positive T permits the exact scalar normalization. The scalar normalization lemma itself applies to any real total.

Conversely, meanPredict_limitNoRegret_of_mean_converges supplies the nonpositive limit for every real comparator and hence every unit comparator.

Divide only by the proved positive high and low horizons. Both horizons diverge, and the reciprocal correction tends to zero.

The first squared loss is at most 1, so 5+4 log T is an upper bound for positive T. Divide by T and use 1/T and log T/T tending to zero. steps.fallback: A vanishing upper bound gives the comparator-wise eventual epsilon property, not an ordinary-limit existence result.

steps.title: Transfer the two-sided best-regret limit
steps.detail: For positive T, divide the exact identity by T. The accepted half-initialized best-regret theorem gives its normalized limit zero, using an actual nonnegative half-FTL loss gap and an upper bound. The fixed correction c divided by T also tends to zero. Adding these two limits and using eventual equality proves the result; an upper bound alone would not suffice. The half-initial lower-control chain proves a prediction-loss gap by empirical-mean minimality and then identifies the feasible minimum. This is a property of this predictor, not nonnegative regret for arbitrary algorithms.
steps.fallback: A proved half-initial ordinary limit and a constant-over-horizon correction give the general-initial ordinary best-regret limit.

notation.meaning: F(A,B,eta)=A/(2 eta)+eta B/2 and S(A,B)=sqrt(A)/sqrt(B) are total real formulas. In each comparison, A and B stay fixed while eta ranges over positive real numbers. The function definitions alone assert no optimizer outside that domain.

R is the distance from one fixed comparator to the initial point; B is the squared-gradient-energy scalar of the fixed run. D is a diameter bound and G names the source L. For each fixed positive coefficient pair, the library compares every positive competitor eta. It does not assert one step simultaneously optimizes all comparators or recomputed trajectories.

The gap and lower bound need A,B>=0 and eta>0. Positive attainment and uniqueness need A,B>0. Distance tuning needs R,B>0; diameter tuning needs finite D,G>0 and natural T>=1. These positivity restrictions are explicit library qualifications of the printed formulas. One-zero cases admit strict improvement; both-zero is constant. Totalized division at eta=0 and T=0 supplies no admissible algorithm step.

On an actual run the gradients depend on eta through the iterates, and the source also warns about unavailable future information. This calculation concerns the coarser two-term expression after dropping the nonpositive terminal-distance term. The full OGD theorem retains that term and its own hypotheses.

notation.meaning: Scale direction: Fix c>0, write x′=x/c and f′(y)=f(cy). Loss output units stay fixed. The concrete source uses c=1000; arbitrary positive c is a library generalization. Unit exponents: The additive-group model represents the ratio [eta]=[x]^2/[loss]. It does not assert eta is never dimensionless: the ratio cancels when [loss]=[x]^2.

Matched history policy: The transformed policy maps every prior loss back by inverse composition, multiplies every history point by c, maps the current loss back, applies the same original policy, then multiplies its selected vector by c. This is an explicit coupling of full mathematical loss-function inputs, not equivalence of independently chosen supports. The policy type receives finite past loss functions, the whole iterate history and the current loss. It has no explicit future/comparator/horizon argument, but this does not prove independence from external parameters used to choose the policy, initialization or schedule. The transport theorems pair the same chosen original policy with its explicitly constructed counterpart.

Source rounds and whole space: Source rounds1 throughT correspond to Lean rounds0 throughT-1; Lean output T is the source terminal point x_(T+1). V is the whole finite-dimensional real inner-product space. No arbitrary-domain projection-transport theorem is claimed. Boundary cases: The gradient chain rule allows every real c, including0 and negative c. Inverse and path results retain c>0; the canary refutes inverse transport at0. The source eta=1/sqrt(T) requires T>0. The fixed-positive-rate library result also allows T=0. Retained but nonessential restrictions are disclosed per declaration.

Totalized identities and finite bounds: Loss-value and regret-transport equalities allow arbitrary extended-real losses. EReal.toReal maps infinities to a totalized real value; those equalities alone are not finite-loss performance claims. The sharp bound separately requires positive constant eta, whole-space proper/subdifferentiable losses and legal actual feedback. Two source displays: The printed21 unit sanity check uses the relaxed two-term bound. The earlier full Theorem2.13 and its subgradient proof transfer retain the negative terminal squared-distance term. The library sharp bound preserves it and is separately labeled.

pseudocode.title: Transport one chosen full-history policy
pseudocode.intro: Fix c>0, a whole-space initial point, an arbitrary real schedule and loss sequence, and one chosen policy p. Define the transformed policy on every supplied finite history. The path identity is structural; legality and positive-rate assumptions are needed separately for the regret bound.
pseudocode.formula_label: Complete policy transport and paired updates
pseudocode.fallback: Undo the coordinate change in every supplied past loss and the current loss, restore every supplied history point, including the current point, apply the same policy p, then multiply its answer by c. Divide the numerical step by c squared.
lines: Choose c > 0, initial point x0, real schedule eta, losses f, and one policy p.
Set transformed loss f_prime[t](y) = f[t](c * y) and initial point y0 = x0 / c.
Set transformed schedule eta_prime[t] = eta[t] / c^2.
To evaluate p_prime at time t, supply past losses F_prime indexed by Fin t, the full iterate history h_prime indexed by Fin(t+1), and current loss q_prime:
inverse-compose every F_prime[i] and q_prime with multiplication by 1/c;
multiply every h_prime[i], including the current point, by c; apply the same p at time t to these restored inputs;
multiply that selected vector by c and return it.
In each whole-space run at time t, output its current point, then receive its current whole loss, select feedback using its full supplied history, and update by its paired schedule.
The paired outputs satisfy y[t] = x[t] / c; legality is a separate transported property.
